title: Stripping Paint: Methylene Chloride Can Kill
summary: Many paint strippers and solvents contain methylene chloride. Breathing it can kill you within minutes, and long-term exposure can cause cancer and other serious health problems. Check the label and ask for a safer product.
talking_points: Many liquid strippers and solvents for paint removal and bathtub refinishing contain methylene chloride (MeCl). One worker died stripping paint from a church baptismal font in a tight, unventilated space with no respirator and inadequate protective clothing.
Check the label and safety data sheet for 'methylene chloride,' 'dichloromethane,' or 'methylene dichloride.' Your employer must train you on how to work safely with toxic chemicals.
Do not work alone. Make sure the work area is properly ventilated.

If MeCl must be used, your employer must give you PPE: gloves made of polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) or polyethylene/ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH) laminate, or other gloves the maker rates for methylene chloride, face shield or chemical goggles, NIOSH-certified supplied-air respirators, and MeCl-resistant aprons, sleeves, and boots or shoe covers.
Ask for safer products. Less toxic strippers are available that work just as well and cost about the same.
Long-term effects include cancer, brain and nervous system damage, heart problems for those with heart disease, and fertility problems.
Headache, nausea, irritated eyes, nose, and throat, skin irritation or burns, and dizziness or sleepiness can be signs you have already felt the effects. Tell your supervisor.
OSHA requires employers to follow its Methylene Chloride standard. If you think you are in danger, contact your supervisor or union, or call OSHA at 1-800-321-6742.
site_hazards_to_check: Strippers or solvents with methylene chloride on the label or SDS
Small, enclosed, or unventilated spaces such as bathrooms, tanks, and fonts
Missing respirators, gloves, or protective clothing rated for methylene chloride
No training on the hazards of the product
discussion_questions: Does any product we are using today contain methylene chloride? How do you know?
Where could we get a safer product for this job?
What do we do if someone feels dizzy or sick while stripping?
